fuentes/their-number-become-thinned/titu.texto: Their Number Become Thinned: Native American Population Dynamics in Eastern North America

fuentes/their-number-become-thinned/resu.texto: Dobyns studies the Indigenous population of eastern North America, above all Florida, and proposes about 18 million inhabitants north of Mexico around 1500. His central argument is that epidemics of European origin spread across the continent before direct contact and depopulated regions that Europeans saw only in their remains.

fuentes/their-number-become-thinned/por_.texto: He pushed the high-count school to its extreme; David Henige and others objected that those pre-contact epidemics and their mortality rates are assumed without documents that record them.

fuentes/essays-in-population-history/tit.texto: Essays in Population History: Mexico and the Caribbean

fuentes/essays-in-population-history/sop.texto: Three volumes, written with Woodrow Borah

fuentes/essays-in-population-history/res.texto: Gathers Cook and Borah’s studies of the population of Mexico, the Caribbean, and California, based on tribute assessments, visitas, census lists, and parish registers. It includes their estimate of between seven and eight million inhabitants for Hispaniola in 1492, much higher than those of other authors, and studies of colonial diet and mortality.

fuentes/essays-in-population-history/por.texto: It is the major work of the Berkeley school; its coefficients for converting tributaries into inhabitants and its figures for Hispaniola are the main target of criticism by Henige and Livi Bacci.

fuentes/numbers-from-nowhere/titulo.texto: Numbers from Nowhere: The Debate over the Indigenous American Population at the Time of Contact

fuentes/numbers-from-nowhere/resumen.texto: Henige examines how the high estimates of the American population in 1492 were built: the figures of chroniclers, the coefficients, the assumed rates of depopulation, and the epidemics before contact. He argues that the data do not allow those figures to be known and that many estimates turn conjectures into precise numbers.

fuentes/numbers-from-nowhere/por_que_imp.texto: It is the most cited methodological critique of the high figures; defenders of the estimates reproach it for a total skepticism that prevents even giving ranges, which tribute documents allow to narrow.

fuentes/mccaa-1995/titulo.texto: Spanish and Nahuatl Views of Smallpox and Demographic Catastrophe in Mexico

fuentes/mccaa-1995/soporte.texto: Article in the Journal of Interdisciplinary History, vol. 25

fuentes/mccaa-1995/resumen.texto: The demographer Robert McCaa compares Spanish and Nahuatl-language accounts of the smallpox of 1520 and the epidemics that followed in Mexico, and uses them to discuss the weight of disease against war, hunger, and exploitation in the population collapse.

fuentes/mccaa-1995/por_que_importa.texto: It shows that the catastrophe appears in the sources from both sides and discusses how much each cause weighed according to each.

fuentes/mccaa-1995/leer.0.titulo.texto: Author's version, without notes or bibliography (Robert McCaa's website, University of Minnesota)

fuentes/virgin-soil-epidemics-crosby/tit.texto: Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation of America

fuentes/virgin-soil-epidemics-crosby/sop.texto: Article in The William and Mary Quarterly

fuentes/virgin-soil-epidemics-crosby/res.texto: Crosby calls “virgin soil epidemics” those that strike populations never previously exposed to a disease, and argues that smallpox, measles, and other European and African infections caused extraordinary mortality in America because of that lack of prior exposure, worsened by the social disorganization they brought.

fuentes/virgin-soil-epidemics-crosby/por.texto: It became the standard explanation of Indigenous mortality; David S. Jones (2003) objected that its later use turned it into an almost genetic explanation that set aside war, hunger, and forced labor.

fuentes/virgin-soils-revisited/soporte.texto: Article in The William and Mary Quarterly

fuentes/virgin-soils-revisited/resumen.texto: The physician and historian David S. Jones revisits the idea of virgin soil epidemics. He argues that there is no evidence of an inherited immunological weakness specific to Indigenous people and that the very high mortality depended on the conditions created by colonization: war, displacement, hunger, slavery, and forced labor, which also worsen any infection.

fuentes/virgin-soils-revisited/por_que_i.texto: It returned the social causes of mortality to the center of the debate without denying the role of disease.

fuentes/koch-2019/titulo.texto: Impacts on the Terrestrial System of the Arrival of Europeans and the Great Die-Off in the Americas after 1492

fuentes/koch-2019/autor.texto: Alexander Koch, Chris Brierley, Mark M. Maslin, and Simon L. Lewis

fuentes/koch-2019/soporte.texto: Article in Quaternary Science Reviews, vol. 207

fuentes/koch-2019/resumen.texto: The authors, from University College London, gather regional population estimates and propose about 60 million inhabitants in the Americas around 1492 and a drop close to 90% by about 1600. They calculate that about 56 million hectares of cultivated land were abandoned and returned to vegetation, which absorbed enough carbon to explain part of the drop in atmospheric CO₂ recorded in Antarctic ice around 1610 and of the cooling of the Little Ice Age.

fuentes/koch-2019/por_que_importa.texto: It linked the American demographic catastrophe with global climate; other researchers debate how much it weighed against natural factors such as volcanoes and solar activity.

fuentes/koch-2019/leer.0.titulo.texto: Open-access article in Quaternary Science Reviews

fuentes/defining-the-anthropocene/autor.texto: Simon L. Lewis and Mark A. Maslin

fuentes/defining-the-anthropocene/resume.texto: Lewis and Maslin propose setting the start of the Anthropocene at 1610, when Antarctic ice records a minimum of atmospheric carbon dioxide, which they call the “Orbis spike” (“of the world”). They attribute it to the reforestation of the lands left by Indigenous people who died after 1492 and present it as the geological mark of the Columbian Exchange.

fuentes/defining-the-anthropocene/por_qu.texto: Their proposal was not adopted: the Anthropocene working group preferred the mid-20th century, and in 2024 the International Union of Geological Sciences rejected formalizing the Anthropocene as an epoch.

fuentes/lemkin-historian-americas/titulo.texto: Raphael Lemkin as a Historian of Genocide in the Americas

fuentes/lemkin-historian-americas/autor.texto: Michael A. McDonnell and A. Dirk Moses

fuentes/lemkin-historian-americas/soport.texto: Article in the Journal of Genocide Research, vol. 7

fuentes/lemkin-historian-americas/resume.texto: Studies the unpublished manuscripts of Raphael Lemkin, the jurist who coined the word “genocide” in 1944, for a world history of genocide. Lemkin included the Spanish conquest of America among his cases, relying above all on Las Casas, and in it he distinguished physical destruction from cultural destruction.

fuentes/lemkin-historian-americas/por_qu.texto: It shows that the creator of the concept already applied it to the colonization of America, although his broad definition is not the one that was adopted in the 1948 Convention.

fuentes/american-holocaust/titulo.texto: American Holocaust: Columbus and the Conquest of the New World

fuentes/american-holocaust/resumen.texto: Stannard describes American societies before 1492 and the massacres, enslavement, and epidemics that followed, and calculates that about 100 million people died. He argues that the Spanish conquest and Anglo-American colonization were a deliberate genocide, fueled by Christian and European attitudes toward sex, race, and war.

fuentes/american-holocaust/por_que_impor.texto: Published for the quincentennial, it is the main work for the thesis of a continental genocide; its critics object that it uses the highest population figures and attributes to intent what was largely mortality from epidemics.

fuentes/a-little-matter-of-genocide/titu.texto: A Little Matter of Genocide: Holocaust and Denial in the Americas, 1492 to the Present

fuentes/a-little-matter-of-genocide/resu.texto: Essays by Ward Churchill arguing that the destruction of the Indigenous peoples of America was a genocide comparable to or greater than the Holocaust, and that academia and governments deny it. It includes claims, such as that the U.S. Army deliberately distributed blankets infected with smallpox among the Mandan in 1837, that a University of Colorado committee found fabricated in 2006.

fuentes/a-little-matter-of-genocide/por_.texto: It was widely read in Indigenous activism and ethnic studies; after the 2006 report it also became an example of how undocumented claims entered the discussion of genocide.

fuentes/informe-sobre-ward-churchill-200.texto: Report of the Investigative Committee on the Allegations of Academic Misconduct against Professor Ward Churchill
Investigative Committee of the University of Colorado at Boulder

A committee of five professors, two of them from other universities, examined seven allegations against Churchill and concluded that he had fabricated evidence, among it the claim that the U.S. Army deliberately spread smallpox to the Mandan at Fort Clark in 1837; that he had falsified the content of laws such as the 1887 allotment act; and that he had plagiarized others’ texts. Its members recommended sanctions ranging from suspension to dismissal.

It is the central document in the case that ended with Churchill’s dismissal in 2007; his defenders argued that the investigation was retaliation for his political views, and a 2009 jury partly agreed with him, awarding a symbolic one dollar in damages, which the judge overturned.
Committee report, official PDF of the University of Colorado (2015 copy in the Wayback Machine)

fuentes/lewy-2004/titulo.texto: Were American Indians the Victims of Genocide?

fuentes/lewy-2004/resumen.texto: Lewy argues that most of the fall in the Indigenous population of the United States was due to epidemics that no one sought, and that the 1948 Convention requires the intent to destroy a group as such. He concludes that most wars and massacres do not meet that definition, although some episodes, such as certain massacres in California or the Sand Creek massacre (1864), could.

fuentes/lewy-2004/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most cited critique of the general use of the term genocide for North America; its critics object to an overly narrow reading of intent and to its sidelining of the weight of violence, hunger, and forced removals.

fuentes/lewy-2004/leer.0.titulo.texto: Article on the Commentary magazine website

fuentes/the-other-slavery/titulo.texto: The Other Slavery: The Uncovered Story of Indian Enslavement in America

fuentes/the-other-slavery/resumen.texto: Reséndez reconstructs the enslavement of Indigenous people in the Americas, from Columbus’s shipments of Taíno and the slave raids of the Caribbean to debt peonage in Mexico and the captives of New Mexico and California in the 19th century. He estimates that between 2.5 and 5 million Indigenous people were enslaved between 1492 and 1900, largely after the Spanish Crown banned Indigenous slavery in 1542, through disguised forms, and he argues that in the Caribbean, between 1492 and 1550, slavery, overwork, and hunger killed more Indigenous people than epidemics did.

fuentes/the-other-slavery/por_que_import.texto: It won the Bancroft Prize in 2017 and opened the debate on the weight of slavery in the demographic decline; it also documents the capture and sale of captives by Indigenous peoples such as the Comanches and the Utes.

fuentes/milicia-y-descripcion-de-las-ind.texto: Militia and Description of the Indies

A manual for the captains who led “entradas” of conquest and pacification, with instructions on choosing soldiers, weapons, marching, ambushes, war against Indigenous peoples, and founding towns, followed by a description of the Indies. It was written by a veteran of the campaigns of the Kingdom of New Granada.
It is a direct source on how frontier war was waged at the end of the 16th century, told by someone who practiced it and defended it.
1892 edition, vol. 1, Internet Archive (University of Toronto)
1892 edition, vol. 2, Internet Archive (University of Toronto)

fuentes/apologias-y-discursos-vargas-mac.texto: Apologies and Discourses on the Western Conquests

A point-by-point rebuttal of Las Casas’s Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, in which Vargas Machuca accuses the Dominican of exaggerating the figures and the cruelty of the conquistadors, of ignoring the sacrifices, cannibalism, and wars of the Indigenous peoples, and of giving arguments to Spain’s enemies. It remained in manuscript and was not published until 1879.
It is the most complete defense of the conquistadors written by one of them; it shows that the controversy over Las Casas began in his own century.

fuentes/el-padre-las-casas-menendez-pida.texto: Father Las Casas: His Double Personality

A critical biography in which Menéndez Pidal presents Las Casas as a man of fixed ideas who distorted the facts and whose accusations fed propaganda against Spain, and he even attributes paranoid traits to him. In contrast, he defends the work of the Crown and of the other religious orders in the Indies.

It was the most famous critique of Las Casas in the 20th century; Lewis Hanke and other specialists answered that it judged the Dominican by anachronistic criteria and set aside the documents that confirm many of his denunciations.

fuentes/la-encomienda-indiana/resumen.texto: A study of the encomienda as an institution: its origin in the Antillean repartimientos, the legislation that regulated or limited it, from the Laws of Burgos to the New Laws and their partial revocation, and the gap between those norms and the practice of the encomenderos.

fuentes/la-encomienda-indiana/por_que_im.texto: It opened the documentary study of the institutions of Indigenous labor, which Zavala continued with personal service and slavery.

fuentes/aristotle-and-the-american-india.texto: A study of the application of Aristotle’s theory of natural servitude to the Indigenous peoples of America, from the first debates of the 16th century to the Valladolid debate of 1550, with the arguments of Sepúlveda and Las Casas.
It placed the Spanish discussion of the nature of Indigenous people within the history of racial prejudice; it complements The Spanish Struggle for Justice in the Conquest of America.

fuentes/the-old-world-and-the-new/titulo.texto: The Old World and the New, 1492-1650

fuentes/the-old-world-and-the-new/resume.texto: An essay on how America changed Europe: the difficulty Europeans had in understanding the new with their old categories, the effect of silver on the economy and on Spain’s power, and the debates over the nature of Indigenous people and the justice of the conquest.

fuentes/the-old-world-and-the-new/por_qu.texto: It is a brief classic on America’s impact on European thought and economy.

fuentes/empires-of-the-atlantic-world/ti.texto: Empires of the Atlantic World: Britain and Spain in America, 1492-1830

fuentes/empires-of-the-atlantic-world/re.texto: A systematic comparison of Spanish and British colonization: their motives, their treatment of Indigenous peoples, African slavery, religion, government, Creole society, and independence. It argues that the Spanish incorporated Indigenous people as subjects and tributaries within their society, while British colonists tended to displace and exclude them.

fuentes/empires-of-the-atlantic-world/po.texto: It is one of the most cited comparisons of the two colonizations, treating the violence and institutions of both by the same criteria.

fuentes/spains-road-to-empire/titulo.texto: Spain’s Road to Empire: The Making of a World Power, 1492-1763

fuentes/spains-road-to-empire/resumen.texto: Kamen argues that the Spanish empire was not a creation of Castile alone but an enterprise in which Genoese and German bankers, Italian soldiers and Flemings, Portuguese sailors, and Indigenous allies took part, and that Spain was more an organizer than a power dominant in its own right.

fuentes/spains-road-to-empire/por_que_im.texto: It challenged the nationalist view of the empire, both the one that celebrates it and the one that condemns it; its critics object that it underestimates the capacity of Castile itself.

fuentes/seven-myths-of-the-spanish-conqu.texto: The Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest

Restall discusses seven ideas inherited from the accounts of the conquistadors: that it was the work of exceptional men; that it was carried out by an army of the king; that it was only a matter of whites (leaving aside Indigenous allies and Africans); that it ended quickly; that there was total lack of communication; that Indigenous peoples were left paralyzed and desolate; and that the Spanish triumphed through cultural superiority.
He summarized for the general public the historiography that showed the role of Indigenous allies and of disease; some critics object that he replaces one set of myths with opposing generalizations.

fuentes/la-conquista-de-america-todorov/.texto: The Conquest of America: The Question of the Other

Essay that reads the writings of Columbus, Cortés, Las Casas, Durán and Sahagún as ways of discovering, understanding, dominating and knowing the other. It argues that the Spanish won in part through their handling of signs and communication, a thesis that many historians disputed.
It was very influential outside professional history; specialists criticized its idea of a Mexica incapacity to communicate and its use of the chronicles as if they were direct testimony.

fuentes/the-fall-of-natural-man/titulo.texto: The Fall of Natural Man: The American Indian and the Origins of Comparative Ethnology

fuentes/the-fall-of-natural-man/resumen.texto: Study of how Spanish theologians and jurists of the 16th century, from Vitoria and Sepúlveda to Las Casas and José de Acosta, classified American Indigenous peoples using the categories of Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas, and of how that discussion led to comparing peoples and ranking them by their degree of civilization.

fuentes/the-fall-of-natural-man/por_que_.texto: It showed that the Spanish debate over the Indigenous peoples was one of the origins of comparative anthropology.

fuentes/la-filosofia-nahuatl/titulo.texto: Nahuatl Philosophy Studied in Its Sources

fuentes/la-filosofia-nahuatl/resumen.texto: León-Portilla gathers and translates Nahuatl texts recorded after the conquest, above all by Sahagún and his Indigenous collaborators, and argues that they reveal an original thought about divinity, humanity, time and truth: that of the tlamatinime, or wise men.

fuentes/la-filosofia-nahuatl/por_que_imp.texto: It was decisive for assessing Indigenous thought; some critics point out that these texts passed through the filter of Christian friars and students, and that calling it philosophy is an interpretation.

fuentes/history-of-the-conquest-of-peru/.texto: History of the Conquest of Peru

Two-volume history of the Inca empire and of the conquest of Peru up to La Gasca’s pacification, based on chronicles and documents copied from Spanish archives. It presents the Incas as a paternal despotism and the conquistadors as brave and greedy men.
For a century it was the standard version in English and in translation; today it is read as a document of Romantic historiography.

fuentes/1491-mann/titulo.texto: 1491: New Revelations of the Americas Before Columbus

fuentes/1491-mann/resumen.texto: Mann gathers research from previous decades on the Americas before 1492: the high population figures, the antiquity of settlement, cities and agriculture, and the management of the landscape with fire and crops in the Amazon and in North America, which Europeans took for virgin nature.

fuentes/1491-mann/por_que_importa.texto: It was a popular success; some specialists object that it presents as established hypotheses that are still debated, such as Dobyns’s figures.

fuentes/1493-mann/titulo.texto: 1493: Uncovering the New World Columbus Created

fuentes/1493-mann/resumen.texto: Popularization of the Columbian Exchange on a global scale: the plants, animals, diseases and people that crossed the Atlantic and the Pacific after 1492, American silver in China, the potato in Europe, and the trade in Africans.

fuentes/1493-mann/por_que_importa.texto: It updated Crosby’s work for the general public with later research.

fuentes/the-columbian-exchange/titulo.texto: The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492

fuentes/the-columbian-exchange/resumen.texto: Crosby studies the transfer of plants, animals and diseases between America and the Old World after 1492: smallpox and other epidemics that decimated Indigenous peoples, the horses, cows and pigs that multiplied in America, and maize, potatoes and cassava that increased the population of Europe, Africa and Asia.

fuentes/the-columbian-exchange/por_que_i.texto: It gave the phenomenon its name and brought biology into the history of the conquest; the book, rejected at first by several publishers, became a classic of environmental history.

fuentes/ecological-imperialism/titulo.texto: Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900

fuentes/ecological-imperialism/resumen.texto: Crosby argues that Europeans prevailed above all in the temperate regions, such as the Río de la Plata, North America, Australia and New Zealand, which he calls “neo-Europes,” because they arrived with a set of plants, animals, weeds and diseases that transformed those environments and displaced the native populations.

fuentes/ecological-imperialism/por_que_i.texto: It extended the Columbian Exchange thesis to the European colonization of the whole world; its critics reproach it for a biological determinism that pushes human decisions into the background.

fuentes/guns-germs-and-steel/resumen.texto: Diamond argues that Eurasia dominated America and other regions because of geographic advantages: more domesticable species of plants and animals, an east–west axis that facilitated their diffusion, and, from living alongside livestock, diseases against which Eurasians had some resistance. He uses the capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca as an example of those distant causes.

fuentes/guns-germs-and-steel/por_que_imp.texto: It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1998 and popularized the explanation of the conquest through germs; historians and anthropologists object that it is a geographic determinism that leaves little room for politics, Indigenous alliances and the decisions of individuals.

fuentes/harner-1977/titulo.texto: The Ecological Basis for Aztec Sacrifice

fuentes/harner-1977/resumen.texto: Harner argues that Mexica human sacrifice—which, citing an estimate by Woodrow Borah, he puts at some 250,000 victims a year in central Mexico in the 15th century—and the consumption of parts of the sacrificed bodies were responses to a shortage of animal protein in the densely populated Valley of Mexico.

fuentes/harner-1977/por_que_importa.texto: It opened a widely discussed debate; almost all specialists rejected the thesis on the basis of the data on the Mexica diet, and because ritual consumption was limited and did not relieve any shortage.

fuentes/ortiz-de-montellano-1978/resumen.texto: A response to Harner: with the data from the chronicles on the Mexica diet, which included maize, beans, amaranth, chia, birds, dogs, insects, fish and algae, he shows that protein was not lacking and that the consumption of meat from the sacrificed was concentrated in harvest times and among the nobility, not in times of shortage.

fuentes/ortiz-de-montellano-1978/por_que.texto: It is the most cited refutation of the ecological explanation of sacrifice.

fuentes/cannibals-and-kings/titulo.texto: Cannibals and Kings: The Origins of Cultures

fuentes/cannibals-and-kings/resumen.texto: Essay in materialist anthropology that explains institutions such as war, sacrifice, food taboos and the State by the pressure of population on resources. One chapter adopts Harner’s thesis on Mexica sacrifice and cannibalism as a response to the lack of protein.

fuentes/cannibals-and-kings/por_que_impo.texto: It spread the ecological explanation of Mexica sacrifice beyond academia.

fuentes/the-man-eating-myth/titulo.texto: The Man-Eating Myth: Anthropology and Anthropophagy

fuentes/the-man-eating-myth/resumen.texto: Arens reviews accounts of cannibalism, from Columbus’s Caribs and Hans Staden’s Tupinambá to the Mexica and to peoples of Africa and Oceania, and argues that there is no reliable testimony from a direct observer of cannibalism as an accepted custom. He concludes that the accusation of cannibalism was above all a way of defining other peoples as inferior.

fuentes/the-man-eating-myth/por_que_impo.texto: It provoked a long debate; most anthropologists and archaeologists rejected his general conclusion, citing concordant testimony, twentieth-century ethnographies and archaeological findings, though they accepted his warning about self-interested accusations.

fuentes/three-cheers-for-hans-staden/tit.texto: Three Cheers for Hans Staden: The Case of Brazilian Cannibalism

fuentes/three-cheers-for-hans-staden/res.texto: A response to Arens: Forsyth compares Staden’s account with those of Léry, Thevet, Anchieta and the letters of the Jesuits, written by authors of different nations, religions and interests, and shows that they agree on the details of the Tupinambá ritual of executing and consuming prisoners.

fuentes/three-cheers-for-hans-staden/por.texto: It is the most cited documentary argument for holding that Tupinambá ritual anthropophagy existed.

fuentes/consuming-grief/titulo.texto: Consuming Grief: Compassionate Cannibalism in an Amazonian Society

fuentes/consuming-grief/resumen.texto: Ethnography of the Wari’ of Rondônia, in the Brazilian Amazon, who until the 1960s ate parts of the bodies of their own dead as part of mourning. It is based on interviews with people who practiced it and who explain the meaning they gave it.

fuentes/consuming-grief/por_que_importa.texto: It is a case of funerary cannibalism documented by direct testimony, which contradicts Arens’s thesis.

fuentes/war-before-civilization/titulo.texto: War Before Civilization: The Myth of the Peaceful Savage

fuentes/war-before-civilization/resumen.texto: Keeley gathers archaeological and ethnographic data, among them the Crow Creek massacre in South Dakota, to argue that war was frequent in societies without a state and that, in proportion to population, it killed more than the wars of modern states.

fuentes/war-before-civilization/por_que_.texto: It challenged the idea of a peaceful past before civilization; critics such as Douglas Fry and R. Brian Ferguson object that his samples mix homicides, vendettas and wars, and include peoples already altered by colonial contact.

fuentes/beyond-war-fry/titulo.texto: Beyond War: The Human Potential for Peace

fuentes/beyond-war-fry/resumen.texto: The anthropologist Douglas Fry argues that war is not universal in human history: many hunter-gatherer societies did not practice it, and organized violence increases with sedentism, hierarchy and competition for resources.

fuentes/beyond-war-fry/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main response to Keeley; critics object that it minimizes the archaeological evidence of violence in societies without a state.

fuentes/the-ecological-indian/titulo.texto: The Ecological Indian: Myth and History

fuentes/the-ecological-indian/resumen.texto: The anthropologist Shepard Krech examines the image of the Indian as a natural conservationist through concrete cases: the use of fire to modify the landscape, the hunting of bison by driving them over cliffs, and the hunting of beavers and deer for the fur trade. He concludes that Indigenous peoples transformed and managed their environment, but not always according to conservation criteria.

fuentes/the-ecological-indian/por_que_im.texto: It provoked a debate in which Indigenous intellectuals objected that his book served those who denied rights over lands and resources; others read it as a critique of the stereotype of the noble savage.

fuentes/the-myth-of-the-noble-savage/tit.texto: The Myth of the Noble Savage

fuentes/the-myth-of-the-noble-savage/res.texto: The anthropologist Ter Ellingson traces the expression “noble savage”: it appears in the lawyer and traveler Marc Lescarbot (1609) and in the poet John Dryden (1672), but Rousseau did not use it, and it became popular in 1859, when John Crawfurd attributed it to Rousseau at the Ethnological Society of London in order to ridicule those who defended colonized peoples.

fuentes/the-myth-of-the-noble-savage/por.texto: It distinguishes the idealization of Indigenous peoples in older texts from the later label, used to disqualify that idealization.

fuentes/des-cannibales/soporte.texto: Chapter 31 of Book I of the Essays

fuentes/des-cannibales/resumen.texto: Montaigne describes the Tupinambá of Brazil based on what a man who had lived in Antarctic France told him and on his conversation with three Indigenous people brought to Rouen in 1562. He admits that they kill and eat their prisoners of war, but argues that this is less barbarous than torturing men alive, as was done in the Wars of Religion in France, and that each person calls barbarism whatever is not part of his own customs.

fuentes/des-cannibales/por_que_importa.texto: It is considered one of the founding texts of European cultural relativism and of the idealization of the Indigenous as a critique of Europe; it describes ritual anthropophagy without denying it.

fuentes/des-coches/soporte.texto: Chapter 6 of Book III of the Essays

fuentes/des-coches/resumen.texto: In an essay that begins by talking about carriages, Montaigne condemns the conquest of Mexico and Peru: he laments that those peoples were not conquered by Greeks or Romans, who would have refined their virtues, and accuses the Spaniards of having destroyed cities and killed millions for gold and trade. He takes his data from López de Gómara.

fuentes/des-coches/por_que_importa.texto: It spread in France the moral condemnation of the Spanish conquest, one of the literary strands of the Black Legend.

fuentes/segundo-tratado-sobre-el-gobiern.texto: Second part of the Two Treatises of Government, published without an author’s name and dated 1690

Locke grounds property in labor: land belongs to whoever fences it and cultivates it. He uses America as an example of the state of nature (“at the beginning all the world was America”) and argues that its lands, in his view uncultivated, yielded little, so that an Indigenous king lived worse than an English day laborer.

It is a central work of liberalism; several historians, such as James Tully and Barbara Arneil, have pointed out that its argument about uncultivated land served to justify the appropriation of Indigenous lands by English settlers.

fuentes/constituciones-fundamentales-de-.texto: Constitution for the colony of Carolina prepared for its Lords Proprietors, of which a draft in the handwriting of John Locke, then their secretary, survives. It established a colonial aristocracy and religious tolerance, and gave every free man “absolute power and authority” over his Black slaves.
It shows Locke’s participation in organizing a plantation colony with slaves; it was never fully applied, and how much of its text is Locke’s work is disputed.
English text at the Avalon Project, Yale University

fuentes/moeurs-des-sauvages-ameriquains/.texto: Customs of the American Savages Compared with the Customs of Earliest Times

Lafitau describes the institutions of the Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) and Hurons, such as descent through the maternal line, the role of women in choosing chiefs, councils, war and the torture of prisoners, and compares them with those of the Greeks, Romans and other ancient peoples. He uses the comparison to argue that all peoples derive from a common revelation.
He is considered one of the precursors of comparative ethnology because of his method of comparing societies instead of judging them as savage.
1724 edition, vol. 1, Internet Archive (John Carter Brown Library)

fuentes/histoire-naturelle-buffon/resume.texto: Encyclopedia of natural history by the intendant of the Jardin du Roi. In volume IX (1761) Buffon argues that American animals are fewer in number and smaller than those of the Old World, and that domestic animals degenerated when taken there because of the cold, damp climate; he described Indigenous peoples as weak and not numerous.

fuentes/histoire-naturelle-buffon/por_qu.texto: His thesis of the inferiority of American nature opened the dispute over the New World; Jefferson replied with measurements of North American animals and sent him the remains of a moose.

fuentes/histoire-naturelle-buffon/leer.0.texto: Œuvres complètes, vol. 1 (Théorie de la Terre, Histoire naturelle), Internet Archive (University of Toronto)

fuentes/recherches-philosophiques-sur-le.texto: De Pauw takes Buffon’s thesis to the extreme: he states that America’s climate degenerated animals and humans, that Indigenous peoples were weak, insensitive and incapable of progress, and that the Creoles born there also degenerated. He further denies that the Mexica and the Incas had cities and laws such as the Spanish chroniclers described.
It provoked replies from Pernety and from the expelled American Jesuits, such as Clavijero and Molina, who wrote their histories partly to refute him.

fuentes/histoire-des-deux-indes/titulo.texto: A Philosophical and Political History of the Settlements and Trade of the Europeans in the East and West Indies

fuentes/histoire-des-deux-indes/soporte.texto: Expanded in 1774 and 1780 with passages by Diderot

fuentes/histoire-des-deux-indes/resumen.texto: History of European expansion in Asia and America that condemns the cruelty of the conquistadors, the enslavement of Africans and the commercial monopoly, and announces that the enslaved will find an avenger. At the same time it repeats the idea of the degeneration of America and of its inhabitants.

fuentes/histoire-des-deux-indes/por_que_.texto: It was one of the most widely read books of the Enlightenment, banned in France and in Spain, and a source of the Enlightenment condemnation of colonization and the slave trade.

fuentes/history-of-america-robertson/res.texto: History of the discovery and conquest of America by the Spanish, written with documents that the author obtained from Spain through British diplomats. It describes Indigenous peoples as societies at a lower stage of social progress, and judges the conquest with more moderation than Raynal, although it criticizes Spanish greed and intolerance.

fuentes/history-of-america-robertson/por.texto: The Royal Academy of History proposed translating it, but the government of Charles III halted the translation and commissioned Juan Bautista Muñoz to write a history of its own based on documents.

fuentes/reflexiones-imparciales-nuix/tit.texto: Impartial Reflections on the Humanity of the Spaniards in the Indies

fuentes/reflexiones-imparciales-nuix/sop.texto: Castilian translation by Pedro Varela y Ulloa, Madrid, 1782

fuentes/reflexiones-imparciales-nuix/res.texto: Nuix responds to Raynal and Robertson: he argues that the deaths of Indigenous people were due above all to epidemics and to the vices of the Indigenous themselves, that the Crown and the Church protected the Indigenous with their laws, and that other powers, such as England and the Netherlands, treated the peoples they colonized worse.

fuentes/reflexiones-imparciales-nuix/por.texto: It is one of the first systematic defenses of Spanish colonization against the Enlightenment, a precursor of what in the 20th century was called the White Legend.

fuentes/reflexiones-imparciales-nuix/lee.texto: 1782 Spanish translation, Internet Archive (John Carter Brown Library)

fuentes/historia-del-nuevo-mundo-munoz/s.texto: Only the first volume was published

fuentes/historia-del-nuevo-mundo-munoz/r.texto: First volume of the history of America commissioned by Charles III from Muñoz, which reaches up to 1500. It is based on the documents Muñoz gathered in Spanish archives and criticizes the foreign authors who wrote without them.

fuentes/historia-del-nuevo-mundo-munoz/p.texto: His search for documents led to the creation of the General Archive of the Indies in 1785; the collection of copies he left is still a source for the history of the conquest.

fuentes/la-disputa-del-nuevo-mundo/titul.texto: The Dispute of the New World: The History of a Polemic, 1750–1900

fuentes/la-disputa-del-nuevo-mundo/sopor.texto: Spanish translation: Fondo de Cultura Económica, Mexico, 1960

fuentes/la-disputa-del-nuevo-mundo/resum.texto: Gerbi reconstructs the controversy over the supposed inferiority of American nature and of American men: Buffon, De Pauw, Raynal and Robertson; the replies of the expelled American Jesuits, of Jefferson, of Alexander Hamilton and of Humboldt; and the ideas of Kant and Hegel about America.

fuentes/la-disputa-del-nuevo-mundo/por_q.texto: It is the classic study of the dispute; it shows how the American responses to Buffon and De Pauw also became a defense of their own land.

fuentes/the-atlantic-slave-trade-a-censu.texto: The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census

First systematic calculation of the number of Africans taken to America, made from published data on imports and exports. It estimated some 9.5 million people landed between the 15th and 19th centuries.
It replaced the figures of 15 to 20 million that circulated without documentary basis and opened the quantitative study of the trade; the later database revised his figure upward.

fuentes/trans-atlantic-slave-trade-datab.texto: Voyages: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database
Database on CD-ROM (1999) and online (2008), directed by David Eltis and David Richardson

It brings together data on more than 36,000 slave-ship voyages, with their flag, ports, dates and the number of captives embarked and disembarked, taken from archives in Europe, Africa and America. Its estimates put some 12.5 million Africans embarked between 1501 and 1866, and some 10.7 million arriving alive in America.
It is the basis of current figures on the trade; it makes it possible to compare the share of each power and of each destination region.

fuentes/atlas-of-the-transatlantic-slave.texto: Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade

Maps and tables produced from the slave-trade database: embarkation regions in Africa, routes, mortality during the crossing, and destinations. According to its estimates, Brazil received close to 45% of the Africans disembarked; the British, French, Dutch and Danish colonies of the Caribbean and the Guianas together almost another 40%; Spanish America around 12%; and continental North America less than 4%.
It presents in accessible form the figures that historians of the trade use today.

fuentes/real-cedula-de-1770/titulo.texto: Real cédula on Teaching Castilian to the Indians

fuentes/real-cedula-de-1770/resumen.texto: Cédula of May 10, 1770, which, at the request of the archbishop of Mexico, Francisco Antonio de Lorenzana, ordered that Castilian be taught to Indigenous people and that measures be taken so that their languages ceased to be used in the American dominions. It reversed the policy of the 16th and 17th centuries, which had combined orders to teach Castilian with evangelization in the general languages.

fuentes/real-cedula-de-1770/por_que_impo.texto: It marks the shift from evangelization in Indigenous languages to Castilianization; its application was slow and limited, and at the end of the colonial period most Indigenous people still spoke their languages.

fuentes/telling-tongues/titulo.texto: Telling Tongues: Language Policy in Mexico, from Colony to Nation

fuentes/telling-tongues/resumen.texto: The linguist Shirley Brice Heath studies language policy in Mexico since the conquest: evangelization in Nahuatl and other languages, the chairs of Indigenous languages, the orders to teach Castilian that were repeated without being carried out, the turn of 1770, and the school-based Castilianization of the 19th and 20th centuries.

fuentes/telling-tongues/por_que_importa.texto: It is the standard study of how and when Castilian was imposed in Mexico.

fuentes/bay-psalm-book/autor.texto: Richard Mather, John Eliot and Thomas Welde

fuentes/bay-psalm-book/resumen.texto: Verse translation of the Psalms made by Puritan ministers of Massachusetts to be sung in their churches, printed by Stephen Daye at the Cambridge press, the first in British America.

fuentes/bay-psalm-book/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first book printed in the English colonies of North America, a century after the first one printed in Mexico.

fuentes/bay-psalm-book/leer.0.titulo.texto: Facsimile reprint of the first edition (1640), published in 1905, Internet Archive

fuentes/johnson-v-mcintosh/autor.texto: Supreme Court of the United States

fuentes/johnson-v-mcintosh/resumen.texto: Unanimous ruling written by the president of the Court, John Marshall, in a lawsuit over lands bought from the Illinois and the Piankashaw in 1773 and 1775. It held that European “discovery” gave the discovering power, and later the United States, dominion over Indigenous lands, and that Indigenous peoples kept only a right of occupancy that only the government could purchase or extinguish.

fuentes/johnson-v-mcintosh/por_que_impor.texto: It is the legal origin of the “doctrine of discovery,” later cited by courts in Canada, Australia and New Zealand and criticized by Indigenous movements.

fuentes/nota-sobre-la-doctrina-del-descu.texto: Joint Note on the Doctrine of Discovery
Dicastery for Culture and Education and Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development

Note of March 30, 2023, in which the Holy See rejected the “doctrine of discovery” and stated that it is not part of Catholic teaching. It held that the papal bulls of the 15th century, such as Inter caetera, were never considered expressions of the Catholic faith and that their content was manipulated for political ends by the competing colonial powers. It acknowledged the abuses suffered by Indigenous peoples, without formally revoking the bulls.
It was the Vatican’s response to the request by Indigenous peoples of Canada and other countries that it revoke the conquest bulls.
English text in the bulletin of the Holy See Press Office

fuentes/discurso-de-francisco-en-santa-c.texto: Address of Pope Francis at the Second World Meeting of Popular Movements

Address of July 9, 2015, in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, in which Francis “humbly asked forgiveness, not only for the offenses of the Church itself but for the crimes against the Indigenous peoples during the so-called conquest of America.” He also recalled the bishops, priests and laypeople who defended Indigenous people.
It is the most explicit papal request for forgiveness for the conquest; some critics judged it unfair to the work of the Church, and others found it insufficient.
Text on the Holy See website

fuentes/decreto-dia-de-la-raza-1917/titu.texto: Decree Declaring October 12 a National Holiday

fuentes/decreto-dia-de-la-raza-1917/resu.texto: Decree of President Hipólito Yrigoyen, of October 4, 1917, which declared October 12 a national holiday in honor of Spain and the discovery of America. It followed the proposal of the Unión Iberoamericana of Madrid to celebrate a “fiesta de la raza,” in the sense of a Hispanic cultural community.

fuentes/decreto-dia-de-la-raza-1917/por_.texto: Argentina was one of the first countries to establish the holiday; the name Día de la Raza became widespread in Spanish America from then on.

fuentes/ley-18-1987-fiesta-nacional/titu.texto: Law 18/1987, establishing October 12 as the National Holiday of Spain

fuentes/ley-18-1987-fiesta-nacional/resu.texto: Law of October 7, 1987, which set October 12 as the National Holiday of Spain. Its preamble justifies the date because on it Spain began a period of linguistic and cultural projection beyond European borders.

fuentes/ley-18-1987-fiesta-nacional/por_.texto: It left the official name as National Holiday; the name Día de la Hispanidad, adopted in 1958, remained in use.

fuentes/ley-18-1987-fiesta-nacional/leer.texto: Text in the Boletín Oficial del Estado

fuentes/decreto-1584-2010/resumen.texto: Decree of November 2, 2010, which reorganized Argentina’s national holidays and renamed October 12 from Día de la Raza to Día del Respeto a la Diversidad Cultural, to dedicate it to historical reflection and intercultural dialogue.

fuentes/decreto-1584-2010/por_que_import.texto: It expresses the change of official view of the conquest in Argentina; its critics saw it as an ideological revision, and its defenders as the recognition of Indigenous peoples.

fuentes/defensa-de-la-hispanidad/resumen.texto: Essay presenting the conquest and colonization of America as a Catholic mission: Spain would have brought the faith and the idea of the equality of all men before God to the American peoples, and Hispanidad would be a spiritual community of the peoples of Hispanic language and faith, opposed to liberalism and the Protestant Reformation.

fuentes/defensa-de-la-hispanidad/por_que.texto: It was the founding text of twentieth-century political Hispanism, which inspired Francoism and the Catholic nationalists of Argentina; its critics object that it idealizes the conquest and leaves out violence and exploitation.

fuentes/espana-frente-a-europa/resumen.texto: Bueno argues that Spain must be thought of as an empire and not only as a European nation, and he distinguishes “predatory” empires, which exploit subjugated peoples without incorporating them, from “generative” ones, which create new political societies in the conquered territories. He places the Spanish empire among the latter, because of the miscegenation, the cities and the universities it left behind.

fuentes/espana-frente-a-europa/por_que_i.texto: His distinction is much cited by current Hispanism; critics point out that the Spanish empire was both generative and predatory, as the tribute, the mita and the population decline show.

fuentes/las-venas-abiertas-de-america-la.texto: Essay that traces Latin American history as a continuous plunder of its resources, from the silver of Potosí and the sugar of Brazil to exploitation by British and American companies, framed by dependency theory. It mixes historical data, chronicle and denunciation.

It was widely read by the Latin American left and was banned by the dictatorships of Uruguay, Chile and Argentina. The Manual of the Perfect Latin American Idiot (1996) called it “the bible of the idiot,” and in 2014 Galeano himself said that he could no longer read it and that when he wrote it he did not have the necessary training, though he did not regret it.

fuentes/forjando-patria/resumen.texto: Gamio argues that Mexico was not yet a nation because its Indigenous peoples lived apart by language, culture and poverty, and he proposes studying them with anthropology in order to integrate them into a mestizo nation, with education and economic development.

fuentes/forjando-patria/por_que_importa.texto: It is the founding text of Mexican state indigenismo; from the 1970s on, anthropologists such as Guillermo Bonfil Batalla criticized that its integration project sought to dissolve Indigenous cultures.

fuentes/declaracion-de-barbados/titulo.texto: Declaration of Barbados: For the Liberation of the Indigenous Person

fuentes/declaracion-de-barbados/autor.texto: Symposium on Inter-Ethnic Friction in South America

fuentes/declaracion-de-barbados/resumen.texto: Declaration signed in January 1971 by anthropologists meeting in Barbados, among them Guillermo Bonfil Batalla and Darcy Ribeiro, at a symposium convened by the World Council of Churches and the University of Bern. It accused states, religious missions and anthropology of collaborating with the domination of Indigenous peoples and held that these peoples should be the protagonists of their own liberation.

fuentes/declaracion-de-barbados/por_que_.texto: It marked the break with integrationist indigenismo and anticipated the organized Indigenous movements of the following decades.

fuentes/declaracion-de-barbados/leer.0.t.texto: Text of the First Declaration of Barbados (Institute of Latin American Studies, UFSC)

fuentes/ensayos-de-montaigne/resumen.texto: Three books and 107 chapters that Montaigne wrote, published and revised from about 1570 to 1592: they appeared in 1580, were expanded in 1588, and their last additions, published posthumously, came out in 1595. They speak of himself and of very varied subjects, with a skepticism rooted in Pyrrhonism. Two well-known chapters deal with America: “Of Cannibals” (I, 31) and “Of Coaches” (III, 6), where he deplores the suffering that colonization brought to the Indigenous peoples.

fuentes/ensayos-de-montaigne/por_que_imp.texto: It is the work from which two of the most cited texts on the Indigenous peoples of America in Europe at the time come, and it shows how Montaigne used the American peoples and the conquest to criticize European cruelty, including that of the wars of religion.

personas/william-h-prescott/resumen.texto: American historian who, almost blind, wrote the History of the Conquest of Mexico (1843) and the History of the Conquest of Peru (1847) using copies of documents from Spanish archives, without traveling to America. His books fixed for a century, in English, the image of a conquest carried out by a few Spaniards against exotic empires.

personas/john-h-elliott/resumen.texto: British historian of Spain in the 16th and 17th centuries, professor in London, Princeton and Oxford. In The Old World and the New (1970) he studied the effect of America on Europe, and in Empires of the Atlantic World (2006) he compared British and Spanish colonization.

personas/henry-kamen/resumen.texto: British historian born in Rangoon, a specialist in early modern Spain, who worked for many years at the CSIC in Barcelona. He argues that the Spanish empire was a multinational enterprise, carried out with capital, soldiers and technicians from many peoples, and he discusses both the Black Legend and nationalist exaltation.

personas/benjamin-keen/resumen.texto: American historian of Latin America. Between 1969 and 1971 he debated Lewis Hanke in the Hispanic American Historical Review: he argued that the exploitation of Indigenous labor was structural, and that putting protective laws at the center built a “White Legend.”

personas/ricardo-garcia-carcel/resumen.texto: Spanish historian of early modern Spain, professor at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, author of The Black Legend: History and Opinion (1992), where he distinguishes propaganda against Spain from internal criticism and documented facts.

personas/ramon-menendez-pidal/resumen.texto: Spanish philologist and historian, director of the Royal Spanish Academy. In Father Las Casas: His Double Personality (1963) he attacked Las Casas as a zealot who distorted the facts, a book that specialists on Las Casas, such as Lewis Hanke, criticized for its lack of balance.

personas/silvio-zavala/resumen.texto: Mexican historian trained in Madrid, a scholar of the institutions of the conquest: the encomienda, the personal service of Indians, slavery and the legal ideas that justified or limited them. He showed with documents the gap between the protective laws and their application.

personas/charles-gibson/resumen.texto: American historian who studied the Indigenous peoples of the Valley of Mexico under Spanish rule, using administrative documents and documents in Nahuatl. He showed the continuity of Indigenous peoples, of their cabildos and their nobility, together with the loss of land, tribute and population decline.

personas/james-lockhart/resumen.texto: American historian, professor at the University of California, Los Angeles. He studied the conquistadors of Peru and, using documents written in Nahuatl by Indigenous people themselves, Nahua society after the conquest (The Nahuas after the Conquest, 1992).

personas/miguel-leon-portilla/resumen.texto: Mexican historian of Nahuatl culture, a disciple of Ángel María Garibay. He published Nahuatl Philosophy (1956) and The Broken Spears (Visión de los vencidos, 1959), and in 1984 he proposed calling the fifth centenary of 1492 “encounter of two worlds.”

personas/tzvetan-todorov/resumen.texto: Franco-Bulgarian essayist. In The Conquest of America: The Question of the Other (1982) he read the chronicles of Columbus, Cortés, Las Casas and Sahagún as a case of encounter with the other, and dedicated the book to the memory of a Maya woman who, according to Landa, was thrown to the dogs.

personas/anthony-pagden/resumen.texto: British historian of ideas, author of The Fall of Natural Man (1982), on how Spanish theologians and jurists debated the nature of the American Indigenous peoples.

personas/matthew-restall/resumen.texto: British-American historian at Pennsylvania State University, a specialist in colonial Maya and in the conquest. In The Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003) he discussed the accounts inherited from the conquistadors themselves.

personas/andres-resendez/resumen.texto: Mexican historian at the University of California, Davis. In The Other Slavery (2016) he studied the enslavement of Indigenous people in America, legal and illegal, from Columbus to the 20th century.

personas/charles-c-mann/resumen.texto: American science journalist who popularized, in 1491 (2005) and 1493 (2011), recent research on the population, cities and agriculture of the Americas before Columbus and on the Columbian Exchange.

personas/sherburne-f-cook/resumen.texto: Physiologist at the University of California, Berkeley who, with Woodrow Borah and Lesley B. Simpson, formed the so-called Berkeley school of historical demography: he estimated the population of California, central Mexico and Hispaniola from tribute assessments, visitas and censuses.

personas/woodrow-borah/resumen.texto: Historian at the University of California, Berkeley. With Sherburne F. Cook he estimated the population of central Mexico at about 25 million in 1518 and studied its decline; he also wrote the history of the Juzgado General de Indios de la Nueva España.

personas/massimo-livi-bacci/resumen.texto: Italian demographer at the University of Florence. He studied the decline of the Indigenous population in Hispaniola, Mexico and the Andes, and argued that epidemics do not suffice to explain it: forced labor, displacement, the appropriation of women and the disorganization of communities also played a role.

personas/alfred-w-crosby/resumen.texto: American historian, professor at the University of Texas at Austin. He coined the expression “Columbian Exchange” (1972) and popularized the idea of “virgin soil epidemics” (1976) to explain Indigenous mortality.

personas/philip-d-curtin/resumen.texto: American historian of Africa and the Atlantic. In The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969) he made the first systematic calculation of the Africans taken to America, about 9.5 million, which later research revised upward.

personas/david-eltis/resumen.texto: Historian at Emory University, in Atlanta, who directed, with David Richardson, the database of Atlantic slave-trade voyages (Voyages, slavevoyages.org), which brings together more than 36,000 documented voyages.

personas/david-stannard/resumen.texto: American historian at the University of Hawaiʻi. In American Holocaust (1992) he argued that the conquest and colonization of America was the greatest genocide in history, with some 100 million deaths.

personas/ward-churchill/resumen.texto: American activist and professor of ethnic studies at the University of Colorado, author of A Little Matter of Genocide (1997). He presented himself as a descendant of Indigenous people, something genealogical research did not confirm. The university dismissed him in 2007, after a committee of his peers concluded in 2006 that he had committed fabrication, falsification and plagiarism in his writings, among them the claim that in 1837 the United States Army gave out smallpox-infected blankets to the Mandan at Fort Clark.

personas/guenter-lewy/resumen.texto: Political scientist and historian born in Breslau, who emigrated from Nazi Germany and taught at the University of Massachusetts. In 2004 he argued that most Indigenous deaths in the United States were due to unintended diseases, and that only some specific episodes could fit the legal definition of genocide. He also disputed that the killings of Armenians in 1915 were a genocide, which earned him strong criticism.

personas/michael-harner/resumen.texto: American anthropologist. In 1977 he proposed that Mexica sacrifice and the ritual consumption of victims responded to a shortage of animal protein, a thesis that most specialists rejected.

personas/marvin-harris/resumen.texto: American anthropologist, founder of cultural materialism. In Cannibals and Kings (1977) he adopted Harner’s ecological explanation of Mexica sacrifice.

personas/william-arens/resumen.texto: American anthropologist at Stony Brook University. In The Man-Eating Myth (1979) he argued that there is no reliable evidence of cannibalism as a custom in any society, and that the accusations served to dehumanize other peoples.

personas/lawrence-keeley/resumen.texto: American archaeologist at the University of Illinois at Chicago. In War Before Civilization (1996) he gathered archaeological and ethnographic data to argue that war was frequent and deadly in societies without a state, against the image of a peaceful past.

personas/michel-de-montaigne/resumen.texto: French essayist, councillor of the parliament and mayor of Bordeaux. In “Of Cannibals” (1580) and “Of Coaches” (1588) he used American Indigenous peoples to criticize European customs, and he condemned the cruelty of the Spanish conquest.

personas/john-locke/resumen.texto: English philosopher. He was secretary to the Lords Proprietors of Carolina and held shares in the Royal African Company, which trafficked in slaves. In the Second Treatise (1689) he used America as an example of the state of nature and of uncultivated land that could be appropriated through labor.

personas/joseph-francois-lafitau/resumen.texto: French Jesuit who lived for five years among the Catholic Iroquois of Kahnawake, near Montreal. In his Customs of the American Savages (1724) he compared their institutions with those of the ancient peoples of Europe.

personas/buffon/resumen.texto: French naturalist, intendant of the Jardin du Roi and author of the Natural History. He held that American nature was weaker than that of the Old World, with smaller animals and fewer species, a thesis that opened the dispute over the New World.

personas/cornelius-de-pauw/resumen.texto: Dutch clergyman and writer, canon at Xanten. In his Philosophical Researches on the Americans (1768–1769) he claimed, without having traveled to America, that its climate degenerated men and animals, and he provoked replies from Pernety, Clavijero and other Americans.

personas/guillaume-raynal/resumen.texto: French abbé and writer, director of the History of the Two Indies (1770), with passages by Diderot, which condemned slavery and the cruelty of the colonizers. The Parlement of Paris ordered the 1780 edition burned, and Raynal had to go into exile.

personas/william-robertson/resumen.texto: Scottish historian, Presbyterian minister and principal of the University of Edinburgh. His History of America (1777) used documents sent to him from Spain; it described Indigenous peoples as societies at a lower stage of social development and criticized the conquest with more moderation than Raynal.

personas/juan-nuix/resumen.texto: Catalan Jesuit expelled with his order in 1767, who lived in Italy. In Impartial Reflections (1780, translated into Castilian in 1782) he defended the conduct of the Spaniards in the Indies against Raynal and Robertson.

personas/juan-bautista-munoz/resumen.texto: Chief cosmographer of the Indies. In 1779 Charles III commissioned from him a documentary history of America, in response to Robertson. To write it he gathered papers from archives throughout Spain, work that led to the creation of the General Archive of the Indies in Seville (1785). He published only the first volume of his History of the New World (1793).

personas/antonello-gerbi/resumen.texto: Italian historian of Jewish origin who, expelled by the racial laws of 1938, lived for ten years in Lima. In The Dispute of the New World (1955) he reconstructed the controversy over the supposed inferiority of American nature and men, from Buffon to Hegel.

personas/bernardo-de-vargas-machuca/resu.texto: Castilian soldier who campaigned against Indigenous peoples in New Granada and was governor of the island of Margarita. He wrote a manual for conquest captains, Militia and Description of the Indies (1599), and, around 1612, a reply to Las Casas’s A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies.

personas/ramiro-de-maeztu/resumen.texto: Spanish writer, ambassador to Argentina from 1928 to 1930. In Defensa de la Hispanidad (1934) he presented Spain’s work in America as a Catholic and universal mission. He was shot by Republican militias in 1936.

personas/gustavo-bueno/resumen.texto: Spanish philosopher, professor at Oviedo and creator of philosophical materialism. In Spain Versus Europe (1999) he distinguished “predatory” empires, which exploit subjugated peoples, from “generative” ones, which incorporate them into their society, and he placed the Spanish empire among the latter.

personas/manuel-gamio/resumen.texto: Mexican anthropologist and archaeologist, a student of Franz Boas, who excavated Teotihuacan. In Forging the Nation (Forjando patria, 1916) he proposed integrating Indigenous people into the mestizo nation, and from 1942 until his death he directed the Inter-American Indigenist Institute.

personas/eduardo-galeano/resumen.texto: Uruguayan journalist and writer, author of Open Veins of Latin America (1971), a reading of Latin American history as the plunder of its resources by empires. In 2014 he said that he could no longer reread it and that when he wrote it he lacked the necessary training in economics.

personas/rigoberta-menchu/resumen.texto: K’iche’ Maya activist from Guatemala and winner of the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992, in the 500th anniversary year of 1492. In 1999 the anthropologist David Stoll showed that parts of her 1983 testimony about her family and the war did not match other data, which opened a debate about the genre of testimony.

personas/andres-manuel-lopez-obrador/res.texto: President of Mexico between 2018 and 2024. In 2019 he asked, in a letter to King Felipe VI and to the pope, that they apologize for the abuses of the conquest; the Spanish government rejected the request.

personas/antoine-joseph-pernety/resumen.texto: French Benedictine who sailed with Bougainville to the Falkland Islands in 1763–1764 and wrote about them and about Santa Catarina Island in Brazil. While serving as librarian to Frederick II in Berlin, he answered De Pauw in 1770 with a dissertation that defended, from his experience as a traveler, the nature and the peoples of the Americas.

personas/faustino-rodriguez-san-pedro/re.texto: Spanish conservative lawyer and politician, mayor of Madrid (1890–1891) and minister in the governments of Silvela and Maura. As president of the Unión Iberoamericana, he proposed in 1913 celebrating October 12 as a “fiesta de la raza” (festival of the race), in the sense of a community of Hispanic peoples.

hechos/debate-demografico-de-la-conquist.texto: The debate over how many people lived in the Americas in 1492

Estimates of the population of the Americas in 1492 range from about 8 million (Alfred Kroeber, 1939) and 13.4 million (Ángel Rosenblat, 1954) to between 90 and 112 million (Henry Dobyns, 1966). The Berkeley school of Cook and Borah proposed about 25 million for central Mexico alone in 1518, and between 7 and 8 million for Hispaniola. The high figures start from tribute assessments and visitation counts multiplied by coefficients (Cook and Borah), or from the later minimum population multiplied by a depopulation rate, with epidemics that would have spread before direct contact (Dobyns). David Henige (1998) argued that there is no data to know, and Massimo Livi Bacci (2003) reduced the population of Hispaniola to a few hundred thousand. The most widely used syntheses, such as that of William Denevan (1992, about 54 million) and that of Koch and others (2019, about 60 million), fall in the middle, and most authors agree on a later decline of between half and more than 90%, depending on the region.

hechos/debate-sobre-las-epidemias-de-sue.texto: The debate over epidemics and other causes of death

The documents record successive epidemics from the smallpox outbreak of 1518–1520: measles, typhus, influenza, the cocoliztli of 1545 and 1576 in Mexico, and later malaria and yellow fever, brought with the African slave trade. Alfred Crosby (1976) explained their mortality by the lack of prior exposure among Indigenous people (“virgin soil”), and Noble David Cook (1998) made epidemics the main cause of the catastrophe. David S. Jones (2003), Livi Bacci and Reséndez argue that war, slavery, forced labor, hunger and flight multiplied that mortality, and they note that on Hispaniola the Taíno population had already fallen sharply well before the smallpox of 1518. On the cocoliztli, Rodolfo Acuña-Soto and others (2002) proposed a local hemorrhagic fever aggravated by drought, and ancient DNA from Teposcolula (Vågene and others, 2018) identified a Salmonella (Paratyphi C) in victims of the 1545 epidemic, possibly arrived from Europe, without ruling out other pathogens.

hechos/gran-mortandad-y-clima/titulo.texto: The great American die-off and the CO₂ minimum of 1610

hechos/gran-mortandad-y-clima/resumen.texto: Antarctic ice cores, such as that of Law Dome, record a drop in atmospheric carbon dioxide of between 7 and 10 parts per million between 1570 and 1620, with a minimum around 1610. Simon Lewis and Mark Maslin (2015) attributed it to the reforestation of cultivated land abandoned after the death of most of the Indigenous population, and Koch and others (2019) calculated that this regrowth absorbed between 47% and 67% of the carbon the atmosphere lost between 1520 and 1610, and contributed to the cooling of the Little Ice Age. Other researchers give more weight to natural causes, such as volcanic eruptions and lower solar activity. The proposal to use 1610 (the “Orbis spike”) as the start of the Anthropocene was not adopted.

hechos/debate-sobre-genocidio-en-america.texto: The debate over whether the conquest of America was a genocide

Raphael Lemkin, who coined the word in 1944, included the Spanish conquest in his drafts of a history of genocide, but the 1948 Convention defined it as acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group as such. David Stannard (1992) and Ward Churchill (1997) applied the term to the conquest and colonization as a whole, while Guenter Lewy (2004) and many historians argue that most deaths were due to unintended epidemics, and that the intent to exterminate can be proven only in specific episodes. The only documented deliberate distribution of blankets from smallpox patients is the one at Fort Pitt (1763), whose effect is uncertain, and the one involving the Mandan in 1837 that Churchill spread was judged by the commission that investigated him to have been invented. Among those episodes, massacres such as those at Jaragua (1503), Mystic (1637) or Sand Creek (1864) are debated, and above all the destruction of the Indigenous peoples of California between 1846 and 1873, which Benjamin Madley (2016) documented massacre by massacre and characterized as genocide under the 1948 definition. Andrés Reséndez, by contrast, stresses the weight of slavery. In 2015 Canada’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission called the residential school policy for Indigenous children “cultural genocide.”

hechos/caso-ward-churchill/resumen.texto: In 2005, after the controversy over an essay of his about September 11, the University of Colorado investigated charges of academic misconduct against Ward Churchill, one of the main defenders of the thesis of American genocide. A faculty committee concluded in 2006 that he had fabricated evidence, such as the deliberate distribution of smallpox blankets by the army among the Mandan in 1837; that he had misrepresented the content of laws such as the 1887 land allotment law; and that he had plagiarized. The university fired him in July 2007. In April 2009 a jury found that his views had weighed on the dismissal and awarded him one dollar in damages, but in July the judge annulled that sum and denied his reinstatement because the university had quasi-judicial immunity. The Colorado Supreme Court upheld that decision in 2012, and the United States Supreme Court declined to review it in 2013.

hechos/esclavitud-indigena-en-america/ti.texto: Indigenous slavery in the Americas, before and after 1492

hechos/esclavitud-indigena-en-america/re.texto: Before 1492 there were slaves in several American societies, such as the tlacotin of the Mexica, the war and debt slaves of the Maya, and those of the peoples of the Northwest Coast of North America. Many peoples took captives, such as the Tupinambá, who kept them until sacrificing them, and the trade in captives among Indigenous peoples continued in the colonial period and grew with European demand. Columbus sent Taíno to be sold in Seville in 1495, and in 1500 the queen ordered that those who had been sold be freed. The Crown permitted enslaving “cannibals” (1503) and rebels in a “just war,” and the New Laws prohibited the enslavement of Indigenous people in Spanish America in 1542, although legal enslavement of the Mapuche continued (1608–1683), along with captures on the frontiers and covert forms such as personal service and debt peonage. Portuguese, English, French and Dutch colonists enslaved Indigenous people under their own laws: the Paulista bandeiras, although Portugal limited this from 1570 to “just war” and the ransom of captives, and banned it in 1755; the Carolina trade (between 24,000 and 51,000 captives between 1670 and 1715, according to Alan Gallay); or the panis of New France. Andrés Reséndez (2016) estimates that between 2.5 and 5 million Indigenous people were enslaved in the Americas between 1492 and 1900.

hechos/trata-atlantica-de-esclavos/titul.texto: The Atlantic trade in enslaved Africans

hechos/trata-atlantica-de-esclavos/resum.texto: According to the database of David Eltis and David Richardson, between 1501 and 1866 about 12.5 million people were embarked in Africa, and about 10.7 million arrived alive in the Americas; nearly one in seven died during the crossing. Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried almost half and British ships more than a quarter, followed by French, Spanish, Dutch, North American and Danish ships. Brazil received about 45%, the British, French, Dutch and Danish Caribbean almost 40%, Spanish America about 12%, and mainland North America less than 4%. Captives were bought on the coast from merchants and African states, which had obtained them through wars, raids, convictions and debts. The trade was banned by Denmark (by a decree of 1792 in force from 1803), Great Britain (1807), the United States (1808) and Brazil (1850). Spain committed in 1817 to prohibit it from 1820, but it continued as contraband toward Cuba and Puerto Rico, where the last voyages arrived in the 1860s.

hechos/leyes-de-indias-y-su-cumplimiento.texto: The laws protecting Indians and their enforcement

The Spanish Crown enacted laws to limit the treatment of Indigenous people: the Laws of Burgos (1512), the New Laws (1542), which prohibited their enslavement and the granting of new encomiendas, the ordinances of 1573, which replaced “conquest” with “pacification,” and the Recopilación of 1680, which gathered these norms, among them those of the protectors of the natives. The same laws organized forced labor by rotation through the repartimiento and the mita. Their application was uneven. In 1545 the clause of the New Laws that abolished encomiendas upon the death of their holder was revoked, after the rebellion of the encomenderos of Peru and protests in Mexico, and the Castilian formula “obedézcase pero no se cumpla” (“obey but do not comply”) allowed a royal order to be suspended while it was appealed. At the same time, Indigenous people litigated extensively in the audiencias and, from 1592, in the General Indian Court of Mexico, and inspections punished some abuses. Charles Gibson (1964) and James Lockhart (1992) showed, with administrative documents and in Nahuatl, that the Nahua peoples kept their own cabildos and nobility while losing land and population. Lewis Hanke stressed the effort toward justice, Silvio Zavala reconstructed how the encomienda and slavery evolved between law and practice, and Benjamin Keen emphasized the distance between the norms and everyday exploitation.

hechos/sacrificio-humano-en-america/resu.texto: Archaeology confirms human sacrifice in many American societies: more than a hundred victims at the Feathered Serpent Pyramid in Teotihuacan (around the year 200), warriors sacrificed at the Huaca de la Luna of the Moche, human offerings in the cenote of Chichén Itzá, some 140 children sacrificed by the Chimú at Huanchaquito-Las Llamas around 1450, the capacocha children of the Incas found at Llullaillaco, and the skulls of men, women and children from the Mexica Huey Tzompantli. Documents describe it among the Mexica, the Maya and the Incas, and the last documented sacrifice north of Mexico was that of a young Oglala woman by the Skidi Pawnee in 1838. What is debated is the number of victims, not whether it occurred.

hechos/debate-sobre-el-sacrificio-mexica.texto: The debate over the scale and meaning of Mexica sacrifice

Diego Durán wrote that at the consecration of the Templo Mayor in 1487, 80,400 people were sacrificed over four days, and Andrés de Tapia estimated 136,000 skulls in the great tzompantli by counting its poles. Many historians, such as Ross Hassig, consider these figures exaggerated, since they would imply about fourteen sacrifices a minute, day and night. Excavations of the Templo Mayor and, since 2015, of the Huey Tzompantli, however, found remains of hundreds of victims, including women and children. Michael Harner (1977), who cited an estimate by Woodrow Borah of some 250,000 victims a year in central Mexico, explained it through protein scarcity, a thesis popularized by Marvin Harris and rejected by Bernard Ortiz de Montellano (1978) and almost all specialists. For Leonardo López Luján and Guilhem Olivier it was a religious and political practice, shared throughout Mesoamerica and linked to war and tribute. Some authors, such as the German Peter Hassler (1992), argued that mass sacrifice was an invention of the conquistadors, a claim archaeology contradicts. Sepúlveda and others used the sacrifices to justify the conquest.

hechos/debate-sobre-el-canibalismo-en-am.texto: The debate over cannibalism in America

Accusations of cannibalism began with Columbus and the physician Diego Álvarez Chanca, who called the Caribs of the Lesser Antilles “cannibals,” and they had consequences: in 1503 the Crown authorized enslaving “cannibals.” William Arens (1979) argued that no reliable witness saw cannibalism as a custom, and that the accusation served to dehumanize. Donald Forsyth (1985) replied that the accounts of Staden, Léry, Thevet and the Jesuits on Tupinambá ritual anthropophagy agree, even though their authors had different origins and interests, and Beth Conklin documented funerary cannibalism among the Wari’ of Brazil until the 1960s. Today most specialists accept ritual consumption among the Tupinambá and the Mexica and funerary consumption in some Amazonian peoples. The practice among the ancestral Pueblo peoples of the Southwest is debated, and the general accusation against the Caribs is considered exaggerated or self-interested.

hechos/debate-sobre-la-guerra-prehispani.texto: Archaeology and inscriptions show warfare in the Americas long before 1492: the Crow Creek massacre in South Dakota, where around 1325 almost 500 people were killed and scalped; palisaded villages on the Mississippi; the wars between Tikal and Calakmul recorded on Maya stelae; the scenes of prisoner capture from the Moche; the hilltop fortresses of the Andes before the Incas; and the conquests of the Incas and the Mexica. Lawrence Keeley (1996) used these data against the “myth of the peaceful noble savage” and argued that war killed, proportionally, more than in modern states. Douglas Fry and R. Brian Ferguson objected that he mixes types of violence and societies altered by contact. The data show large differences between regions and periods, with increases in violence associated with droughts, as in the Southwest and the Plains between the 12th and 14th centuries.

hechos/debate-sobre-el-buen-salvaje/titu.texto: The noble savage and its opposite: European images of the American Indian

hechos/debate-sobre-el-buen-salvaje/resu.texto: From Columbus’s letter of 1493, which described the Taíno as gentle people without weapons, Europeans used Indigenous Americans to speak about themselves. Montaigne (1580) and the Baron de Lahontan (1703) presented them as natural men who criticized European corruption, while Sepúlveda and others described them as barbarians who had to be subjected. The expression “noble savage” appears in the English poet John Dryden (1672) and was later attributed to Rousseau, who did not use it. According to Ter Ellingson (2001), John Crawfurd popularized it in 1859 to discredit those who defended colonized peoples. In the 20th century the debate continued with Keeley’s “myth of the peaceful savage” and Shepard Krech’s “ecological Indian.”

hechos/leyenda-negra/titulo.texto: The Black Legend: propaganda against Spain in the 16th and 17th centuries

hechos/leyenda-negra/resumen.texto: During Spain’s wars with the Netherlands, England and France, texts and images against the Spanish monarchy circulated: Reginaldo González Montano’s The Arts of the Inquisition (1567), the Apology of William of Orange (1581), Antonio Pérez’s Relaciones (1594) and, above all, the translations of Las Casas’s A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies into Dutch (1578), French (1579) and English (1583), illustrated by Theodor de Bry in 1598. This propaganda used documented facts, such as the massacres of the conquest and the fall of the Indigenous population, together with exaggerations and omissions, and it was silent about the abuses of the powers that spread it. Unsourced claims also circulated, such as that in Spain it was debated whether Indigenous people had souls, when the Valladolid debate (1550–1551) questioned whether they could be subjected by war. Julián Juderías popularized the expression “Black Legend” in 1914, although Emilia Pardo Bazán had already used it in 1899.
