Historians such as Ricardo García Cárcel and Henry Kamen see it as part of the usual propaganda among powers, and authors such as Philip Powell and Elvira Roca Barea see it as a lasting prejudice.

hechos/leyenda-rosa/titulo.texto: The White Legend: the defense of Spain’s colonial work in America

hechos/leyenda-rosa/resumen.texto: Since Juan Nuix’s reply to Raynal and Robertson (1780), a current defended Spanish colonization by highlighting the laws protecting Indians, the debates on the justice of the conquest, mestizaje, the cities, the universities and hospitals, and the end of human sacrifice. It was continued by the American Charles Lummis (The Spanish Pioneers, 1893) and, in the 20th century, by Ramiro de Maeztu, Rómulo Carbia, Ricardo Levene, for whom the Indies “were not colonies,” Philip Powell and Gustavo Bueno, and in 2016 by Elvira Roca Barea. Its critics, such as Benjamin Keen (“The White Legend Revisited,” 1971) and José Luis Villacañas (Imperiophilia, 2019), object that it takes norms for practice, that it relegates violence, forced labor and the population decline, and that it chooses the sources that suit it.

hechos/polemica-sobre-las-casas/titulo.texto: The controversy over Bartolomé de las Casas

hechos/polemica-sobre-las-casas/resumen.texto: Las Casas published the Brevísima relación in Seville in 1552. He had written it in 1542 to secure the New Laws, and it includes figures such as more than twelve million deaths that come from no count. As early as 1555 the Franciscan Motolinía wrote to Charles V that he exaggerated, that he did not know the Indigenous languages, and that he did not stay to evangelize. Around 1612 Bernardo de Vargas Machuca rebutted him point by point in defense of the conquistadors. In 1963 Ramón Menéndez Pidal described him as a fanatic who distorted the facts and even attributed paranoid traits to him. His defenders, such as Lewis Hanke and Manuel Giménez Fernández, show that many episodes he denounced, such as the Jaragua massacre (1503) and the slave-raiding fleets that captured people in the Lucayas, are attested in other documents. Las Casas himself acknowledged in his Historia de las Indias that he had been wrong in proposing in 1516 that African slaves be brought to relieve the Indigenous people, although the Crown had already permitted bringing them to Hispaniola since 1501, and the trade did not originate with his proposal.

hechos/disputa-del-nuevo-mundo/titulo.texto: The dispute over the New World

hechos/disputa-del-nuevo-mundo/resumen.texto: Buffon (1761) argued that American nature was weaker than that of the Old World, and Cornelius de Pauw (1768) extended this “degeneration” to Indigenous people and Creoles. They were answered by the Benedictine Antoine-Joseph Pernety (1770), by the expelled American Jesuits, such as Francisco Javier Clavijero (1780) and Juan Ignacio Molina, and by Thomas Jefferson in his Notes on the State of Virginia (1785). Raynal and Robertson partly repeated the thesis, and Spain responded by commissioning Juan Bautista Muñoz to write a history based on documents. Antonello Gerbi (1955) reconstructed the whole controversy, and historians see in the responses of the expelled Jesuits one of the expressions of Creole patriotism that preceded the independence movements.

hechos/intercambio-colombino/resumen.texto: From Columbus’s second voyage (1493), which brought horses, cattle, pigs, wheat and sugarcane to Hispaniola, plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic. From America came maize, potatoes, cassava, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco, peanuts and chili peppers, which increased food production in Europe, Africa and Asia. To America came wheat, rice, sugarcane, coffee, citrus fruits, cattle and horses, and also smallpox, measles, typhus and, with the slave trade, malaria and yellow fever. Alfred Crosby (1972) gave it its name. The American origin of syphilis, which appeared in Europe in 1495, is probable but still debated.

hechos/lenguas-generales-y-castellanizac.texto: To evangelize, the Church and the Crown adopted Indigenous “general languages,” such as Nahuatl in New Spain, Quechua and Aymara in the Andes, Guaraní in Paraguay, and Tupí, the “língua geral,” in Brazil. Missionaries wrote their grammars and vocabularies: Olmos (Nahuatl, 1547), Domingo de Santo Tomás (Quechua, 1560), Molina (1571), Anchieta (Tupí, 1595), Valdivia (Mapudungun, 1606), Ruiz de Montoya (Guaraní, 1639) and, in New England, John Eliot with his Bible in the Massachusett language (1663). Charles V had ordered in 1550 that Castilian be taught to them, but around 1580 Philip II ordered the creation of chairs of general language in Lima and Mexico and required that priests serving Indians know it. In 1596 he rejected a proposal from the Council of the Indies to oblige Indigenous people to speak Castilian, although he ordered that teachers be offered to those who wanted to learn it. Policy changed in the 18th century. The Directory of Pombal (1757) imposed Portuguese in the Amazon, and a Real Cédula of Charles III of 1770 ordered Castilianization and the suppression of Indigenous languages, but at the end of the colonial period most Indigenous people still spoke their own languages.

hechos/universidades-de-la-america-colon.texto: Spain founded more than twenty universities in America. Santo Domingo’s obtained a papal bull in 1538, although it is debated from when it actually functioned as one; those of Lima and Mexico were created by royal decrees of 1551, and others followed, among them Bogotá, Quito, Córdoba, Chuquisaca, Guatemala, Cusco, Caracas, Havana and Santiago de Chile. In the English colonies Harvard College was founded in 1636, and an Indian College built around 1655 produced only one Indigenous graduate. William and Mary followed in 1693 and Yale in 1701, and before 1776 there were nine colleges. In New France there was a Jesuit college in Quebec from 1635, and the Seminary of Quebec (1663) became a university only in 1852. Portugal did not allow universities in Brazil, whose students went to Coimbra. The Spanish American universities trained mainly Creoles and Spaniards. Their statutes often excluded Blacks, mulattos and many mestizos, on grounds of illegitimacy or limpieza de sangre. Indigenous people were not excluded, but there were few of them, mostly sons of caciques, who were also educated in their own schools, such as the Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco (1536).

hechos/hospitales-de-la-america-colonial.texto: The first European hospital in America was that of San Nicolás de Bari in Santo Domingo, around 1503. It was followed by the Hospital de la Purísima Concepción, later known as Jesús, founded by Cortés in Mexico around 1524; the Real de Naturales in Mexico (1553), for Indigenous people; and the Hospital de Santa Ana in Lima (1549), as well as the hospital-towns of Vasco de Quiroga in Michoacán. In Brazil the Santa Casa de Misericórdia de Santos opened in 1543. In New France the Augustinian nuns founded the Hôtel-Dieu de Quebec (1639), and Jeanne Mance founded the one in Montreal (1642). In the British colonies the first hospital founded as such was the Pennsylvania Hospital in Philadelphia (1751). They cared for the poor, the sick and travelers with the medicine of the time, and they could not stop the great epidemics.

hechos/imprentas-de-la-america-colonial/.texto: The first printing press in America operated in Mexico from 1539, with Juan Pablos as operator for the Seville house of the Cromberger family. Lima’s began in 1584 with Antonio Ricardo, followed by Puebla (1640), Guatemala (1660), the Guaraní missions (around 1700), Bogotá (1738) and Buenos Aires (1780). In the English colonies the first press arrived in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1638, began printing in 1639, and in 1640 printed the Bay Psalm Book. In New France there was no printing press until the British conquest, and in Brazil the Portuguese Crown closed those that were attempted, until the Impresión Regia (Royal Press) of Rio de Janeiro (1808). Spanish American presses needed licenses and suffered censorship, and they printed many works in Indigenous languages.

hechos/fundacion-de-yale/resumen.texto: The assembly of the Connecticut colony authorized the Collegiate School in 1701, created by Puritan ministers who considered Harvard too liberal. It first operated in Saybrook, moved to New Haven in 1716, and in 1718 took the name Yale after a donor, Elihu Yale, who had made a fortune with the English East India Company.

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-de-pensilv.texto: In 1751 the physician Thomas Bond and Benjamin Franklin obtained from the Pennsylvania assembly the creation of a hospital for poor and mentally ill patients, financed with public funds and private donations. It was the first hospital founded as such in the British colonies of North America.

hechos/fundacion-del-archivo-general-de-.texto: Founding of the General Archive of the Indies

Charles III ordered in 1785 that the documents on the Indies scattered across Simancas, Cádiz and Seville be gathered in the Casa Lonja in Seville, at the proposal of Juan Bautista Muñoz and with the support of minister José de Gálvez. One of its aims was to write the history of America with documents, in contrast to foreign authors such as Robertson and Raynal.

hechos/dia-de-la-raza/titulo.texto: October 12: Día de la Raza, Hispanidad and Diversity Day

hechos/dia-de-la-raza/resumen.texto: The fourth centenary of 1492 was celebrated in 1892 in Spain and in America. In 1913 the former Spanish minister Faustino Rodríguez-San Pedro proposed a “fiesta de la raza” (festival of the race), in the sense of a Hispanic community. Argentina declared it a national holiday by decree of Yrigoyen in 1917, and Spain did so by law in 1918. The United States made Columbus Day a federal holiday in 1937. In Spain it was renamed Día de la Hispanidad in 1958 and Fiesta Nacional in 1987. Since the late 20th century several countries have renamed it: Día del Encuentro de Dos Mundos in Chile (2000), Día de la Resistencia Indígena in Venezuela (2002), Día del Respeto a la Diversidad Cultural in Argentina (2010) and Día de la Descolonización in Bolivia (2011). In 2021 President Biden proclaimed, in the United States, an Indigenous Peoples’ Day alongside Columbus Day.

hechos/hispanismo/resumen.texto: The word “Hispanidad,” proposed according to Maeztu by the priest Zacarías de Vizcarra in Buenos Aires in 1926 to replace “raza,” named the idea of a spiritual community of peoples who spoke Spanish and shared the Catholic faith, which Ramiro de Maeztu set out in Defense of Hispanidad (1934). Francoism adopted it as foreign policy with the Consejo de la Hispanidad (1940), and it had an echo among Argentine Catholic nationalists. Gustavo Bueno (1999) reformulated it from materialism, distinguishing “generative” empires, such as the Spanish, from “predatory” ones, and Elvira Roca Barea (2016) defended the imperial record against the Black Legend. Its critics, such as José Luis Villacañas (2019), argue that it idealizes the conquest and pushes into the background violence, forced labor and Indigenous and African peoples.

hechos/indigenismo/resumen.texto: In the 20th century intellectuals and governments in Latin America championed the Indigenous past and denounced the situation of Indigenous people: Manuel Gamio in Mexico (1916), Luis E. Valcárcel and José Carlos Mariátegui in Peru, and José Vasconcelos with his praise of mestizaje (1925). The Pátzcuaro Congress (1940) created the Inter-American Indigenist Institute, and states founded institutes to integrate Indigenous people through schooling and development. Since the Barbados Declaration (1971), anthropologists and Indigenous organizations have criticized that this indigenismo spoke for Indigenous people and sought to dissolve their cultures into the mestizo nation. Open Veins of Latin America (1971), by Eduardo Galeano, spread in those years a reading of the conquest and the colony as plunder, from which its author distanced himself in 2014.

hechos/congreso-indigenista-de-patzcuaro.texto: Congress held in Pátzcuaro, Michoacán, in April 1940, convened by the government of Lázaro Cárdenas, with delegates from the American countries and Indigenous representatives. It agreed to create the Inter-American Indigenist Institute, which was installed in Mexico in 1942 under the direction of Manuel Gamio, and it recommended that each country create its own indigenist institute.

hechos/quinto-centenario/resumen.texto: The commemoration of 500 years since 1492 divided opinion. In 1984 Miguel León-Portilla proposed calling it an “encounter of two worlds.” Spain organized the Seville Universal Exposition, and the Dominican Republic inaugurated the Columbus Lighthouse in October 1992. Indigenous and left-wing organizations responded with the campaign “500 years of Indigenous, Black and popular resistance,” with meetings such as the one in Quito in 1990. In October 1992 the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the K’iche’ Maya activist Rigoberta Menchú, whose 1983 testimony was later discussed by the anthropologist David Stoll (1999).

hechos/doctrina-del-descubrimiento/resum.texto: In Johnson v. M’Intosh (1823), the Supreme Court of the United States ruled that European discovery had given the colonial powers, and later the United States, dominion over Indigenous lands, leaving Indigenous people only a right of occupancy. The doctrine was later applied in Canada, Australia and New Zealand, and Indigenous movements linked it to the papal bulls of 1493, whose revocation they demanded. In March 2023 the Vatican declared that the doctrine is not part of Catholic teaching and that the bulls were used by the powers for political ends, without repealing them.

hechos/perdon-del-papa-francisco-2015/ti.texto: Pope Francis asks forgiveness for the crimes of the conquest

hechos/perdon-del-papa-francisco-2015/re.texto: In Santa Cruz de la Sierra, on July 9, 2015, Pope Francis asked forgiveness for the offenses of the Church and for the crimes against Indigenous peoples during the conquest of America, and he recalled the religious figures who defended Indigenous people. John Paul II had acknowledged the suffering of Indigenous people in 1992, and in 2022 Francis asked forgiveness in Canada for the role of the Church in residential schools for Indigenous children.

hechos/carta-de-lopez-obrador-2019/titul.texto: Mexico’s request for an apology from Spain

hechos/carta-de-lopez-obrador-2019/resum.texto: In March 2019 Mexican president Andrés Manuel López Obrador sent letters to King Felipe VI and Pope Francis asking them to acknowledge the abuses of the conquest and to apologize. The Spanish government rejected the request and argued that the arrival of the Spaniards should be judged by the standards of their time. The pope acknowledged in 2021 the “sins” committed in the evangelization. In 2024 President Claudia Sheinbaum did not invite the king to her inauguration, because he had not replied to the letter, and Spain did not send a representative.

hechos/traslado-del-monumento-a-colon/ti.texto: The move of the Columbus monument in Buenos Aires

hechos/traslado-del-monumento-a-colon/re.texto: In June 2013 the government of Cristina Fernández de Kirchner began dismantling the Columbus monument behind the Casa Rosada, a gift from the Italian community inaugurated in 1921, to replace it with a statue of Juana Azurduy donated by Bolivia. The Italian community and the city government opposed it, and there was a lawsuit. The Azurduy statue was inaugurated in July 2015, and the Columbus monument was later reassembled on the Costanera Norte, opposite Aeroparque.

hechos/derribo-de-estatuas-de-colon-2020.texto: During the protests over the death of George Floyd, in June 2020, demonstrators beheaded a Columbus statue in Boston, threw another into a lake in Richmond and toppled another in Saint Paul, and several cities removed theirs. In October 2020 the government of Mexico City removed the Columbus statue from the Paseo de la Reforma before an announced protest. Its defenders, among them Italian American organizations, saw in Columbus a symbol of immigration, and its critics saw the beginning of the conquest.

hechos/historiografia-de-la-conquista/ti.texto: Interpretations of the conquest, from Prescott to the new history of the conquest

hechos/historiografia-de-la-conquista/re.texto: William H. Prescott (1843 and 1847) told the conquest of Mexico and Peru as the feat of a few Spaniards against empires he saw as despotic, following Cortés’s letters and the chronicles of the conquistadors. From the mid-20th century, Miguel León-Portilla popularized Nahua accounts in The Broken Spears (1959), Tzvetan Todorov (1982) read the conquest as an encounter with the other, and Anthony Pagden (1982) studied Spanish debates on the nature of Indigenous people. With documents in Nahuatl, Maya and other languages, James Lockhart (1992), Matthew Restall (2003) and the studies gathered by Laura Matthew and Michel Oudijk (2007) showed that tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, such as the Tlaxcalans, fought much of the war for their own ends, and that Indigenous societies were not paralyzed after the defeat. For Restall, the image of a few Spaniards who won alone is a myth inherited from the probanzas with which the conquistadors petitioned the king for favors.

lugares/archivo-general-de-indias/resume.texto: Archive created by Charles III in 1785 in the Casa Lonja in Seville to gather documents on the Indies. It holds the papers of the Council of the Indies, the Casa de Contratación, the audiencias and other bodies concerning Spanish America and the Philippines, and it is the main documentary source for the history of the conquest and colonization. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1987.

lugares/universidad-de-yale/resumen.texto: College founded in 1701 in the Connecticut colony, based in New Haven since 1716, to train ministers and magistrates. It was the third college in the British colonies, after Harvard and William and Mary.

lugares/pennsylvania-hospital/resumen.texto: Philadelphia hospital founded in 1751 by Thomas Bond and Benjamin Franklin for poor and mentally ill patients. It was the first established as such in the British colonies of North America. Construction of its building began in 1755.

lugares/monumento-a-colon-buenos-aires/r.texto: Carrara marble monument by Arnaldo Zocchi, a gift from the Italian community for the centenary of 1810. Its foundation stone was laid in 1910, and it was inaugurated in 1921 behind the Casa Rosada. Dismantled in 2013, it was reassembled on the Costanera Norte, opposite Aeroparque.

lugares/faro-a-colon/resumen.texto: Cross-shaped monument built in Santo Domingo Este to a design by the British architect Joseph Lea Gleave, who won an international competition in 1931. The government of Joaquín Balaguer completed it for the fifth centenary and inaugurated it in October 1992. It holds remains that the Dominican Republic attributes to Columbus, although the cathedral of Seville also claims to have his. Its cost and the evictions of neighboring barrios were widely criticized.
